base.summary: These are the library proof routes for the selected definitions, domain and indicator consequences, Theorem 2.4 and Examples 2.5–2.6. Orabona cites Rockafellar for Theorem 2.4 and leaves the norm example as an exercise.

steps.title: Project the epigraph to the effective domain
steps.detail: Every value below positive infinity has a real upper bound, even when the value is negative infinity. Lift two domain points to real epigraph heights. Convexity combines these lifts; the resulting finite height witnesses domain membership.
steps.fallback: Domain points admit real epigraph heights; their convex combinations do too.

steps.title: Use real values only where finiteness is proved
steps.detail: For Theorem 2.4, the no-negative-infinity hypothesis and domain membership prove that each value is finite. Convexity of the effective domain proves this also for the interpolated point. The real epigraph equivalence then translates the ordinary convexity inequality in both directions. Infinite values are never globally identified with zero.
steps.fallback: Under no-bottom and a convex effective domain, the strict-weight inequality is equivalent to epigraph convexity.

steps.title: Read constraints as epigraph intersections
steps.detail: The indicator epigraph is the product of the feasible set and nonnegative real heights. Adding an indicator intersects the original epigraph with the feasible cylinder; the no-bottom assumption excludes ambiguous infinite addition. Convexity follows from products and intersections of convex sets.
steps.fallback: Indicator convexity is equivalent to convexity of V; adding it restricts the epigraph to V.

steps.title: Check the affine and norm examples
steps.detail: Affine evaluation preserves convex combinations exactly. For the norm, apply the triangle inequality followed by nonnegative homogeneity. The real-valued coercion bridge transfers these inequalities into the same extended-real epigraph definition.
steps.fallback: Affine functions satisfy equality; the norm satisfies the convexity inequality.
